title: Managers and record men fleecing vocal groups like the Clovers
summary: Sam says the same story repeats; the Clovers were paid $250 a week while their manager held the money, and Ridley saw the same.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Yeah, you know. Superstars. But--it's the same thing man, it's the same thing warmed all over when you, you and I were young, coming up, man. And playing in those commercial bands, and traveling on them roads, doing those one-nighters, um, like ah, just like when they get these four--four or five guys off the streets, man, uh, some uh, Jew pass by in his car with the window down and look on and see four or five guys sitting on the stoop humming, 'Come here, sign.' Dig it man, they sure enough this is the area where everything is happening now. Boom. Put the record out; they don't know nothing, man. All they know they, they making records and going on the road. This man is collecting all the money, putting it in--I've seen it man, with the Clovers, man. The Clovers, they had this man, that was traveling with them, I used to see that briefcase, boy used to get--when we started, it be about this size, and there was only two of us you know. Paul Williams. And then half way...that bag used to swell up like this man, you know. Every night. And they was--he was paying them $250 a week, salary. The Clovers, the great 'Mint Julep' Clovers. He was paying them guys. And all that money was going to hell, man.
I worked with the Moon Glows and the
Platters and I saw the same thing.

Alright, so if it's all the same thing, uh, warmed all over, Larry, with his, more electrified Man. It's the same things, it's the same thing which... have nothing to do with the class--with, with the modern jazz-music, you know. Man, because we are over here, just like the classic, classical music string players, you know, is over here, you see. Country and Western is over there. So, man you've got your variety of uh, variety of music. So, uh, uh, people shouldn't be concerned about, you know, uh, uh, the other type of music man. Be concerned about trying to keep--keep our music popular. Like, you know, the classical music, uh, understand was in, in terrible shape here,man,for awhile, man, they're wasn't many people going to concerts--our, our classic, classical orchestra here in the state of New Jersey--tell me it was way down in the money. Everything gets, gets shaken for awhile, man, but, some kind of way, man it will always survives, you know.
